expected_evidence: Geological: platinum-group-element (Pt/Ir) anomaly, elevated nanodiamonds, magnetic and glassy microspherules, and a 'black mat' organic-rich layer dated to ~10,950 BCE across multiple Younger Dryas boundary (YDB) sites in North America, Europe, and elsewhere
Geological/ice-core: chemical spike (ammonium, nitrate, platinum) in Greenland ice cores at the YD onset horizon consistent with an airburst/biomass-burning event

Astronomical: absence of an identifiable crater (expected under an airburst scenario rather than a ground impact), possibly fragments of an impactor or cosmic dust concentration in the relevant sediment layer; candidate structures (e.g., Hiawatha crater) have been proposed but redating has largely ruled them out as contemporaneous — this is model-prior, not confirmed

Material/archaeological: continent-wide charcoal/soot spike indicating widespread wildfires, disruption of Clovis-era lithic technocomplex in North America, and abrupt megafaunal extinction signatures near the YD boundary
Genetic: population bottleneck signals in megafaunal (and possibly early human) lineages coincident with the YD onset

Model-prior: this matches the well-known but contested Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis (Firestone et al. 2007 and successors), which has produced published claimed evidence but also numerous non-replications and methodological critiques — flagging this as an unverified, disputed source rather than settled fact
response.rationale: The event date (~10,950 BCE) sits right at the Younger Dryas onset, so the younger-dryas detectability row is most applicable, with some overlap into upper-paleolithic (comparable geological ~0.6-0.65 and astronomical ~0.7 baseline scores). However, the hypothesis specifies a cosmic AIRBURST rather than a ground impact, which structurally changes the evidence profile: airbursts characteristically leave no crater and only diffuse, easily-degraded chemical/particulate signatures (PGE anomalies, nanodiamonds, spherules) rather than a discrete geological structure. This makes the high astronomical-evidence detectability in the table (0.7) an overestimate for this specific mechanism, since the strongest category of evidence for impacts — a crater — is not expected to exist at all under an airburst model, and candidate structures found (e.g. Hiawatha) have largely been redated away from the YD boundary. Conversely, the geological/sedimentary evidence that IS expected (PGE, spherules, black mats, ice-core spikes) has actually been reported by proponents at many sites globally, indicating this class of evidence is detectable in principle and partially exists already — though its interpretation remains scientifically contested, with multiple independent teams failing to replicate key markers. This pattern (evidence exists and has been actively searched for, but is contested rather than simply absent) argues against invoking low detectability to explain an evidentiary gap; the gap here is one of interpretive controversy, not undetectability. I therefore set the adjustment at 0.5: lower than the table's astronomical figure (since no crater is expected under an airburst) but higher than a pure absence-of-evidence score, reflecting that partial, disputed geological/material evidence has plausibly survived and been reported, while a large expected category (impact structure) is inherently unlikely to exist by mechanism, not by preservation failure.
